Read About Mexico City

A capital built on an island that isn't there anymore, by people who buried their own empire under it on purpose — and it hasn't finished settling since.

The eagle, the cactus, and the empire underneath the plaza

The most accepted date for the founding of Tenochtitlan is March 13, 1325. The Mexica people, wandering south after leaving their homeland of Aztlán, had been told by their god Huitzilopochtli to settle wherever they found an eagle perched on a nopal cactus, devouring a serpent. They found that exact scene on a small island in the middle of Lake Texcoco — unpromising ground, swampy and mostly underwater, which is presumably why nobody else had already taken it. They built anyway, filling the shallows with reed rafts packed with lake mud to make farmable land, and within two centuries that island city had become the capital of an empire of an estimated 200,000 to 250,000 people, larger than most European capitals of the same era.

When Hernán Cortés and his allies took the city in 1521, they didn't relocate the capital — they built directly on top of it, using the same stones from the same temples for their own cathedral and government palace. The sacred precinct at the heart of Tenochtitlan, including the Templo Mayor — the twin-shrined pyramid dedicated to Huitzilopochtli and the rain god Tlaloc — was deliberately buried and paved over. For more than four centuries it stayed that way, known only from Spanish chronicles, sitting directly beneath the Zócalo you're standing in.

It came back by accident. On February 21, 1978, electrical company workers digging near the cathedral hit a carved stone disc nearly 3.5 meters across: the Coyolxauhqui Stone, showing the moon goddess dismembered and decapitated by her brother Huitzilopochtli, dated to around 1473. The find triggered the Templo Mayor Project, led by archaeologist Eduardo Matos Moctezuma, which spent years excavating the pyramid's buried foundations one city block from the cathedral steps. You can walk the ruins today and see, at close range, the exact base the Spanish built over rather than removed.

The staircase Diego Rivera used to rewrite the story

Diego Rivera began painting the grand staircase of the Palacio Nacional in May 1929 and didn't finish until November 1935 — six years on a single stairwell. The result, The History of Mexico, is not a neutral timeline. The central panel crowds pre-Hispanic civilization, Spanish conquest, colonial rule, independence, and revolution into one sweeping composition, with Emiliano Zapata and Karl Marx both making appearances; the side panels work chronologically outward from there. Rivera was a committed Marxist working on commission from a post-revolutionary government eager to tell its own founding story on the walls of its own seat of power, and the murals read that way — the Spanish conquistadors and Porfirio Díaz's dictatorship painted as villains, indigenous civilization and the peasant revolutionaries painted as the through-line of Mexican identity.

The murals are still inside a working government building — the offices of the Mexican presidency occupy the rest of the palace — which is part of what makes the staircase strange to stand in. You are looking at a fresco arguing that the Mexican state exists to correct the injustices of Spanish colonialism, painted on the wall of the actual seat of that state, in a building whose foundations sit on the rubble of Moctezuma's own palace.

Rivera didn't decorate the staircase. He used it to tell the government that commissioned him what its own history was for.

The cathedral of lucha libre

Salvador Lutteroth founded Empresa Mexicana de Lucha Libre in 1933, importing the format from American professional wrestling and adapting it into something distinctly Mexican — full-face masks with mythological or heroic identities, a strict public morality of técnicos (good) against rudos (bad), and a mask that, for the biggest stars, is treated as sacred: losing it in a lucha de apuestas betting match is a career-defining humiliation, and unmasking a wrestler in public is one of the few unbreakable taboos in the sport. Lutteroth's promotion, renamed Consejo Mundial de Lucha Libre in 1991, is the oldest professional wrestling organization still operating anywhere in the world.

Its home since April 1956 is Arena México, a 16,500-seat venue in the Doctores neighborhood that fans call La Catedral de la Lucha Libre — the cathedral of lucha libre. It was purpose-built for wrestling, at a scale nothing in Mexican sports had attempted before, and it still runs weekly cards nearly seven decades later. Sit in the cheap seats on a Tuesday or Friday night, surrounded by families who have been coming for three generations, and the atmosphere reads less like a sports event than a passion play: recognizable moral categories, a costume that is never explained and never needs to be, and thousands of people who already know exactly which side they're on before the bell rings.

A plaza with three names, and one afternoon it can't outrun

Plaza de las Tres Culturas takes its name from the three eras stacked visibly on the same ground: the excavated pyramids of Tlatelolco, the Aztecs' twin city to Tenochtitlan and the site of its final defeat in 1521; the Templo de Santiago, a sixteenth-century church built from the temple's own stones; and the mid-century apartment towers surrounding the square, built in the 1960s as a flagship of modernist urban planning.

On the evening of October 2, 1968 — ten days before Mexico City was due to open the Summer Olympics — the Mexican army and police surrounded a student demonstration in the plaza and opened fire. Estimates of the dead run from the low hundreds into the low thousands, disputed for decades because the government suppressed its own casualty count; the Games opened on schedule ten days later, with the massacre officially unmentioned. It is one of the most contested and least resolved events in modern Mexican history, and it happened on the same few hundred square meters where the Aztec empire had made its own last stand four centuries earlier. The plaza carries a small memorial today. Most tour buses don't stop here. It's worth the detour.

Three eras, one square, and a government that spent decades trying not to talk about the middle one.

A city that has never stopped settling

Tenochtitlan's lake is gone — drained deliberately by Spanish and later Mexican engineers over four centuries, partly to stop catastrophic flooding, partly because a lake made colonial control harder. What's left underneath the modern city is the old lakebed itself: soft, compressible clay, saturated with the aquifer that now supplies most of Mexico City's drinking water. Pumping that aquifer faster than rain can refill it causes the clay to compact, and the ground above it drops. Satellite radar measurements have recorded parts of the city sinking by up to 35 centimeters in a single year — among the fastest urban subsidence rates recorded anywhere on Earth, and wildly uneven, since the old lakebed districts sink far faster than the volcanic-rock neighborhoods at the city's edges.

You can see the unevenness without any instruments. Door frames in the historic center sit slightly off true. Church floors roll instead of running flat. Some Metro platforms have sunk enough relative to their own tunnels that engineers have had to rebuild station entrances to match. None of it reads as a disaster in the moment — it reads as a slight, persistent tilt, the ground admitting, one imperceptible centimeter at a time, that it was a lake before it was a city, and that a lake is what it would rather still be.
